documented_content: European Commission publishes the legislative proposal establishing the digital euro (COM(2023)0369): legal tender status, online and offline use, distribution by payment service providers, ECB may set holding limits (level not specified), no remuneration.
Announcement in Parliament that the proposal is referred to the ECON committee and associated committees.
ECB publishes its formal legal opinion on the proposal (CON/2023/0034), supporting the project and arguing for ECB discretion over holding limits.
ECON rapporteur (Berger) tables a first draft report on the proposal. The text of the draft could not be retrieved; code only what you can infer from the fact of tabling on that day.
LIBE committee adopts its opinion, concerning privacy and data protection only.
Two sets of amendments to the ECON draft report are tabled. Their content could not be retrieved.
Formal resumption of the file after the European elections (procedural decision to continue business from the previous term).
Change of ECON rapporteur: Berger steps down, Navarrete Rojas (same political group) is appointed. The new rapporteur has no publicly documented position on the file at this date.
A new LIBE rapporteur for the opinion is appointed.
LIBE committee adopts a new opinion, concerning privacy and data protection only.

The ECON rapporteur publishes a 27-page chapter in a yearbook, presented as a personal contribution, arguing that the digital euro is not needed and pointing to private European payment solutions (naming the European Payments Initiative) as the alternative.
Eurogroup ministers endorse a framework for how the ceiling on individual holding limits will be set and amended; no numeric limit is agreed.
European Council leaders call for accelerated progress on the digital euro; no design content.
ECB closes the preparation phase and announces the move to the next phase of the project, including preparation for possible issuance.

New ECON draft report: an offline digital euro is introduced immediately; an online digital euro is introduced only if the Commission, after an investigation, concludes that no suitable private pan-European payment solution exists; holding limits made more prescriptive, set by the Commission based on an ECB report.

Council agrees its negotiating position: ECB sets holding limits within an overall ceiling agreed by the Council, reviewed at least every two years; providers may not charge consumers for basic services; guaranteed access for providers to mobile device hardware and software; interchange and merchant fees capped for at least five years at levels of comparable payment means, then cost-based. On the same day four sets of amendments to the ECON draft report are tabled.
ECB publishes a call for payment service providers to express interest in a 12-month pilot planned for the second half of 2027.

ECON committee adopts its position: overall cap on holdings set by the Commission on the ECB's recommendation and reviewed every two years; legal persons may not hold digital euro except incoming payments for up to 24 hours; rollout phase of at least 24 months; merchant and inter-provider fees capped; offline payments free of charge.
The committee report is formally tabled for plenary; content identical to the committee position of 23 June.
Announcement in plenary of the committee's decision to open negotiations (procedural).
Plenary confirms the negotiating mandate on the basis of the committee text.
ECB announces the selection of 36 payment service providers (banks and non-banks) from more than 50 applicants for the pilot.
